items.title: One Seller, Five Inboxes: Operating Customer Support Across Marketplaces Without Losing Threads
items.summary: Most multi-channel support pain is not volume — it is fragmentation. A buyer asks about sizing on one marketplace chat, follows up about shipping on another, and leaves a review mentioning both. The seller answers each inbox in isolation and accidentally gives two different answers. When you run several storefronts, the hardest problem is not answering fast; it is knowing that two conversations are the same conversation. Why marketplace inboxes resist consolidation Each platform guards its chat as an in-app experience: reply templates, response-time scorecards, and search all live inside the platform's own console. Official APIs exist but are uneven — some expose webhooks, some only polling, some rate-limit aggressively during the exact sales events when message volume peaks. So the realistic architecture is not "one inbox to rule them all" but a sync layer that pulls messages from each console into one working view while replies still go out through each platform's rules. The identity problem: same buyer, different accounts Cross-store buyer identity is the core technical challenge. Three signals, in descending order of reliability: Platform user IDs — authoritative within one platform, useless across two. Order and address matching — same shipping address or order phone number strongly implies one buyer; normalize phone formats before comparing, or you will miss half the matches. Behavioral fingerprints — writing style, question patterns, active hours. Weak alone, useful as a tie-breaker. Design rule: identity matching proposes, humans confirm. Auto-merging two different buyers is far more damaging than leaving two threads of the same buyer unmerged for an hour. Merge rules that survive contact with reality Time-window threading. Messages from the same buyer within a short window belong to one conversation, regardless of which storefront they arrived on. Without this, you answer the shipping question and miss that the sizing question is still open. Intent deduplication. If a buyer has asked the same thing in two places, reply once — in the thread where they asked — and reference the other. Answering the same question twice in two inboxes reads as robotic in both. Priority overrides. Paid-not-shipped beats after-sales beats pre-sales beats everything else, no matter which inbox each message sits in. Sellers who triage per-inbox systematically answer the easy inbox first, not the urgent one. One answer, one source. Policies like shipping cutoffs and return windows should live in one place that feeds every channel's reply templates. The "two different answers" failure is almost never a typing mistake; it is two copies of the truth drifting apart. What breaks during big sales events Traffic spikes arrive at the same hour on every platform simultaneously. Three preparations matter more than any tool: pre-write reply templates for the top questions the event will generate (promo mechanics, shipping deadlines, price-match complaints); lower your per-conversation ambition — during peak, fast correct answers to high-intent messages beat thoughtful answers to everything; and decide in advance which channels get human hours and which run on auto-reply plus a callback promise. Measuring a multi-channel operation Cross-store duplicate rate — how many buyer threads were the same underlying question. High values mean your merge rules are too weak. Per-channel response time against each platform's scorecard — because marketplace algorithms punish slow channels independently. Answer consistency — sample cross-store conversations weekly and check the two threads got the same policy answer. Escalation latency — how long a message marked "needs human" waits during peak, per channel. How we run it We build auto-reply tooling for e-commerce sellers who run multiple storefronts under Dingdang CS ; our write-up on built-in reply configuration across seven platforms covers the per-platform template rules and the daily operating rhythm for solo operators.
items.summary_html:
Most multi-channel support pain is not volume — it is fragmentation. A buyer asks about sizing on one marketplace chat, follows up about shipping on another, and leaves a review mentioning both. The seller answers each inbox in isolation and accidentally gives two different answers. When you run several storefronts, the hardest problem is not answering fast; it is knowing that two conversations are the same conversation.

Why marketplace inboxes resist consolidation

Each platform guards its chat as an in-app experience: reply templates, response-time scorecards, and search all live inside the platform's own console. Official APIs exist but are uneven — some expose webhooks, some only polling, some rate-limit aggressively during the exact sales events when message volume peaks. So the realistic architecture is not "one inbox to rule them all" but a sync layer that pulls messages from each console into one working view while replies still go out through each platform's rules.

The identity problem: same buyer, different accounts

Cross-store buyer identity is the core technical challenge. Three signals, in descending order of reliability:

  1. Platform user IDs — authoritative within one platform, useless across two.
  2. Order and address matching — same shipping address or order phone number strongly implies one buyer; normalize phone formats before comparing, or you will miss half the matches.
  3. Behavioral fingerprints — writing style, question patterns, active hours. Weak alone, useful as a tie-breaker.

Design rule: identity matching proposes, humans confirm. Auto-merging two different buyers is far more damaging than leaving two threads of the same buyer unmerged for an hour.

Merge rules that survive contact with reality

Time-window threading. Messages from the same buyer within a short window belong to one conversation, regardless of which storefront they arrived on. Without this, you answer the shipping question and miss that the sizing question is still open.

Intent deduplication. If a buyer has asked the same thing in two places, reply once — in the thread where they asked — and reference the other. Answering the same question twice in two inboxes reads as robotic in both.

Priority overrides. Paid-not-shipped beats after-sales beats pre-sales beats everything else, no matter which inbox each message sits in. Sellers who triage per-inbox systematically answer the easy inbox first, not the urgent one.

One answer, one source. Policies like shipping cutoffs and return windows should live in one place that feeds every channel's reply templates. The "two different answers" failure is almost never a typing mistake; it is two copies of the truth drifting apart.

What breaks during big sales events

Traffic spikes arrive at the same hour on every platform simultaneously. Three preparations matter more than any tool: pre-write reply templates for the top questions the event will generate (promo mechanics, shipping deadlines, price-match complaints); lower your per-conversation ambition — during peak, fast correct answers to high-intent messages beat thoughtful answers to everything; and decide in advance which channels get human hours and which run on auto-reply plus a callback promise.

Measuring a multi-channel operation
  • Cross-store duplicate rate — how many buyer threads were the same underlying question. High values mean your merge rules are too weak.
  • Per-channel response time against each platform's scorecard — because marketplace algorithms punish slow channels independently.
  • Answer consistency — sample cross-store conversations weekly and check the two threads got the same policy answer.
  • Escalation latency — how long a message marked "needs human" waits during peak, per channel.
How we run it

We build auto-reply tooling for e-commerce sellers who run multiple storefronts under Dingdang CS; our write-up on built-in reply configuration across seven platforms covers the per-platform template rules and the daily operating rhythm for solo operators.

items.title: Log Off: One Real Place. One Small Activity. Local Gemma.
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built At 4:00 PM in Kharghar, I gave a local model a deceptively small job: stop offering me choices and choose one real place I could walk to and return from in 30 minutes. The map pipeline found CIDCO Park seven minutes south, the timing code kept the outing inside daylight, and the interface reduced everything to one ticket. That test became Log Off . Log Off turns four quick choices into one reason to close the laptop. You choose your mood, how much time you have, your energy, and whether you are alone. It then: finds real nearby outdoor places from OpenStreetMap; checks walking time, current weather, sunrise, and sunset; asks a local Gemma 4 model for one small activity at a place that actually fits; and shows one ticket with where to go, what to do, when to leave, and when to be back. The model does not decide distances or invent the schedule. Code owns those facts. The goal is to make the screen the shortest part of the experience. Demo Log Off runs locally on a laptop, so there is no hosted demo. Setup and run instructions are in the README. Here is the complete screen flow: 1. Pick what you need from the break. Four compact choices give the planner enough context without turning the break into another questionnaire. 2. Take one ticket and leave the screen. The result gives one real place, one activity, and the leave-by and back-by times calculated by code. Code rahultapase / log-off Log Off Log Off turns a few preferences into one short reason to leave the screen. Pick a mood, the time available, your energy, and whether you are alone. The app finds a real nearby place, works out a safe walking window around daylight and weather, and asks a local Gemma 4 model for one small activity to do there. The result is a single outing ticket with where to go, when to leave, when to be back, and a task that needs no phone, purchase, or equipment. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass . Screenshots How it works Log Off keeps facts and generation separate: Find facts. A typed area or browser location is rounded to three decimal places before the app requests nearby places from OpenStreetMap and daylight and weather data from Open-Meteo. Build a shortlist. Python code calculates walking time and… View on GitHub FastAPI, TypeScript, Vite, local Gemma 4 through Ollama, and 104 backend tests. Repository: github.com/rahultapase/log-off How I Built It Log Off has three deliberate layers: facts, generation, and validation. 1. Facts before AI. A FastAPI backend uses OpenStreetMap for geocoding and nearby places, then Open-Meteo for weather, sunrise, and sunset. Python code rounds outbound coordinates, calculates walking time and compass direction, merges duplicate map entries, and filters out anything that cannot fit the selected time budget. That produces a numbered shortlist of real places. It also decides whether the outing can happen now or should move to just after sunrise. Gemma never calculates any of this. 2. A local Gemma task writer. Gemma 4 E2B runs locally through Ollama. It receives mood, energy, company, weather, and the numbered shortlist, but no coordinates. Its job is narrow: select one candidate ID and return a short, equipment-free activity as structured JSON. I found that the model was much more useful after code supplied a task style for each mood and energy combination. The first prompt often returned variations of "relax in the park." The final prompt asks for a concrete, finishable observation, investigation, movement, or social task. 3. A factual guardrail. Every model response passes through a validator that checks: valid JSON and schema; a place ID from the supplied shortlist; an activity duration that fits after the round-trip walk; invented place or street names; forbidden distances and clock times; and extra safety constraints for darkness and rain. A rejected response gets one repair attempt. If Ollama is unavailable or both attempts fail, a built-in deterministic activity keeps the ticket usable. The explanation visible to the user is also generated from code facts, not from Gemma's free-text reasoning. 4. I measured it. For the main evaluation, I ran 24 combinations of mood, time, company, and energy at 4:00 PM: Result with Gemma 4 E2B Measured value Valid on the first attempt 23 of 24 Fixed on the single retry 1 of 24 Deterministic fallback used 0 of 24 Invented-place runs 0 of 24 Median model-call latency 2.8 seconds Maximum model-call latency 3.2 seconds The most useful failure was not a hallucination. For a social, with-others, low-energy request, Gemma suggested: "Start a simple card game like Uno." It passed the factual validator but needed equipment, despite the prompt. The validator can prove that an answer fits known facts; it cannot yet prove that the idea is good. That distinction is now an explicit limitation instead of a hidden one. 5. I swapped the model. With the same 12 preference sets, gemma3:1b passed 0 of 12 answers on the first attempt. Eleven were repaired and one fell back safely. Gemma 4 was much more reliable, but the open setup let me measure that difference inside the real application. 6. I kept the final screen quiet. The browser interface is TypeScript and Vite. It uses a daylight arc, accessible controls, visible focus states, reduced-motion support, and one final screen designed to be left behind. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? The model does not need my location. Gemma runs on my laptop through Ollama, so no location is sent to a model provider, no model API key is needed, and inference has no per-request fee. I can inspect the full prompt, constrain its role, keep evaluation results locally, and replace the model without redesigning the app. I could test model sizes on the real task. The Gemma 3 and Gemma 4 comparison used the same planner, validator, preference sets, and hardware. I could choose based on measured reliability instead of a general benchmark or pricing page. Open data keeps generation grounded. OpenStreetMap provides inspectable place IDs and geometry, while Open-Meteo provides weather and daylight data under an open licence. Together they let the model write around facts instead of pretending to know the user's surroundings. Open does not automatically mean offline. Place and weather lookups still need the internet. It does mean I can draw a clear privacy boundary: rounded coordinates go to open-data services, while Gemma stays local and never sees them. It also means the failure handling is mine to test, explain, and improve. Limitations The 24-run evaluation is a focused application test, not a general model benchmark. The validator checks facts and safety rules, not taste. The Uno suggestion passed. Weather describes current conditions even when an after-dark outing moves to tomorrow morning. Place and weather lookups need internet access, even though model inference is local. What's next Take Log Off on a real outing, add an equipment-language validator rule, use forecast data for next-morning plans, and compare more small local models on the same evaluation set. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma : Gemma 4 E2B writes the activity locally, and Gemma 3 1B provides the measured comparison.

Result with Gemma 4 E2B Measured value Valid on the first attempt 23 of 24 Fixed on the single retry 1 of 24 Deterministic fallback used 0 of 24 Invented-place runs 0 of 24 Median model-call latency 2.8 seconds Maximum model-call latency 3.2 seconds

6. I kept the final screen quiet. The browser interface is TypeScript and Vite. It uses a daylight arc, accessible controls, visible focus states, reduced-motion support, and one final screen designed to be left behind.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The model does not need my location. Gemma runs on my laptop through Ollama, so no location is sent to a model provider, no model API key is needed, and inference has no per-request fee. I can inspect the full prompt, constrain its role, keep evaluation results locally, and replace the model without redesigning the app.

I could test model sizes on the real task. The Gemma 3 and Gemma 4 comparison used the same planner, validator, preference sets, and hardware. I could choose based on measured reliability instead of a general benchmark or pricing page.

Open data keeps generation grounded. OpenStreetMap provides inspectable place IDs and geometry, while Open-Meteo provides weather and daylight data under an open licence. Together they let the model write around facts instead of pretending to know the user's surroundings.

Open does not automatically mean offline. Place and weather lookups still need the internet. It does mean I can draw a clear privacy boundary: rounded coordinates go to open-data services, while Gemma stays local and never sees them. It also means the failure handling is mine to test, explain, and improve.

Limitations
  • The 24-run evaluation is a focused application test, not a general model benchmark.
  • The validator checks facts and safety rules, not taste. The Uno suggestion passed.
  • Weather describes current conditions even when an after-dark outing moves to tomorrow morning.
  • Place and weather lookups need internet access, even though model inference is local.
What's next

Take Log Off on a real outing, add an equipment-language validator rule, use forecast data for next-morning plans, and compare more small local models on the same evaluation set.

Prize Categories
  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 E2B writes the activity locally, and Gemma 3 1B provides the measured comparison.

items.title: How OpenSeal's Agent Architecture Works
items.summary: Let’s trace one task through OpenSeal. Suppose an agent is preparing a draft and needs approval before an action can send it. We want to see where the task lives, how a worker gets its next step, and what happens while a person reviews it. The example describes a workflow you can build with the right Skills and host setup. We will follow the saved execution path, then check the model and security settings it needs. Follow the durable path The main sequence is prompt or event → Agent or Team → Objective → Run → Turn → Skill action. An Agent or Team owns the Objective, which states a desired outcome. The Objective produces a Run. A Run advances in Turns, and a Turn may call a Skill to act outside the model's reasoning. The draft goal stays in the Objective. The Run records the attempt to reach it. If work has to wait, you can read that Run’s state without keeping the original API request open. Use leases to recover work A worker claims a Turn for a set time. That claim is called a lease. If the worker stops renewing it, the lease ends and the Turn becomes available again. Check this record when a worker stops mid-task. Every stage is saved before it is acted on. Approval waits are saved too. This gives work and review a common place to live across process restarts. Do not read this as a blanket exactly-once guarantee for external tools. Review each Skill's side effects and the service it calls. A restart test should check both the saved Run state and the external result. Check capabilities before calling routes Two OpenSeal services at the same version can expose different operations. The available surface depends on the store contracts, connected components, and complete configuration. curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/capabilities Run creation needs a dispatcher. Approval resolution needs an authorizer. Workforce authoring needs a complete model endpoint, credential, and model name. A missing capability is not merely hidden in the client; the corresponding operation is not served. This lets a thin client work against a local service or a larger embedding host. The terminal client reads what the server advertises and does not own authoritative state. Closing it leaves durable work running. The health endpoint is a weaker check. Its fixed response does not prove that the database, workers, or model provider can complete your task. Keep orchestration state explicit A Run can wait for a dependency, another agent, an approval, or an inbound event. These are different states because they need different responses. Waiting for another Run to finish is not the same as waiting for a person to decide. Agents can ask each other for work through saved requests. The exchange moves through creation, response, completion, and optional completion review. Because those records are stored, the request can outlive the Run that raised it. Agent and Team definitions have saved versions that do not change. Deployments can switch versions, so they can roll back to an earlier one. A proposed change goes through proposal, review, decision, and activation as separate steps. Saving a decision does not activate the change. Govern actions at the Skill boundary Registering a Skill makes its definition known. A binding grants it to an Agent or Team deployment. Team grants and member grants are separate. When policy requires review, the action call stops at a durable approval checkpoint. A missing approval authorizer does not become permission to approve automatically. In local mode, the standalone operator flag enables local decisions and requires a loopback address. Activity events are saved in the same transaction as the state changes they describe. Credential values are resolved when an action runs and kept out of saved state, prompts, and the terminal client. The host boundary remains important: the standalone API supplies neither authentication nor request authorization nor TLS. A host or proxy must add them. Local approval records use user:local, so they cannot tell you which human clicked approve. Put model routing in the right layer Workforce authoring accepts an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. It can point to a compatible LLM gateway that exposes multiple models. The path is OpenSeal authoring → gateway → model provider. The documented authoring setup selects an endpoint, a credential, and one model name. That is not evidence that the core automatically picks a different model for every task. A gateway's routing and fallback rules must be configured and tested separately. This boundary keeps provider access apart from the durable work model. To test another supported model, change the model setup and compare the result while checking that the proposal still follows the review and apply process. Know which execution path you are using The standalone service uses SQLite. PostgreSQL is available through the Go embedding layer, not as a supported standalone storage setting. Projects group objectives for source monitoring and outreach, and Run commands let a team pause, resume, cancel, or intervene. OpenSeal also has a separate HCL runbook path through openseal run. It runs a typed graph in one process and does not share the durable Run lifecycle, approvals, or activity feed. Do not assume that a runbook command inherits the guarantees described for the durable core. A small evaluation plan Now test the draft workflow. Read capabilities, connect the needed worker, and create one small objective. Watch its Run and Turns. Try an allowed action, then an action that needs review. Restart while that review is pending. Check both the saved approval and anything the action changed outside OpenSeal . Write down the state before and after the restart. That comparison will tell you whether the task recovered as expected and where you need another test. Source and setup guide: https://github.com/axiom-studio/openseal

items.title: Salesforce Closes $3.6 Billion Fin Deal, Adding a Fast-Deploy AI Agent to Agentforce
items.summary: Salesforce now sells two ways to put an AI agent on customer support, and it agreed to pay about $3.6 billion to add the one it describes as fast to deploy. The company completed its acquisition of Fin, the Irish-founded business formerly known as Intercom, on September 10, 2026. What Salesforce Bought Fin sells an AI agent that handles customer queries from start to finish across live chat, email, WhatsApp, SMS, voice and Slack. Salesforce says more than 30,000 companies use it and that it resolves 76% of support volume on average. That 76% is Fin’s own figure. Fin’s help documentation defines its resolution rate as the percentage of conversations the agent resolves without human involvement, and it counts a resolution when the customer confirms the answer or exits without requesting further help. Fin renamed itself from Intercom in May 2026, with the Intercom name continuing as the label for its customer service software platform. CEO and co-founder Eoghan McCabe said at signing that he would stay on. He wrote that “little will practically change. I’ll still be CEO, Des will still be running R&D,” a reference to co-founder Des Traynor. Salesforce’s closing announcement says Fin will operate as part of its AI Labs, though Opus Research reports that responsibility for running the business sits within Service Cloud. Salesforce’s June announcement gave a price of approximately $3.6 billion, subject to customary purchase price adjustments, and no revenue figure. The Irish Times, citing Fin’s website, reported more than $400 million in recurring revenue. Simple division puts the price at no more than about nine times that number. An Early Close Ahead of Guidance Salesforce signed the agreement on June 15 and guided to a close in the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2027, which runs from November 2026 through January 2027. The deal closed 87 days after signing, in the third quarter. On its August 26 earnings report, Salesforce had told investors it expected Fin and the Contentful acquisition to close “in the coming weeks.” The same report put a number on what the two deals add. Salesforce said the pending Contentful and Fin acquisitions account for $200 million of the increase in its full-year fiscal 2027 revenue guidance, which now stands at $46.1 billion to $46.4 billion. Both deals close partway through the year, so that figure covers only a partial year of their revenue, and Salesforce did not split it between the two companies. Two Agents for Two Kinds of Buyer Salesforce draws the distinction itself. The closing announcement pairs Fin’s “fast-to-deploy AI agent” with “Agentforce’s deeply customizable platform.” At signing, Salesforce described Fin as offering “fast time-to-value options especially well-suited for SMB and some commercial organizations that need to launch quickly, integrate with existing systems, and deliver measurable outcomes.” Salesforce also has its own packaged service agent. Ten days after signing, on June 25, it announced Agentforce Help Agent with pay-per-resolution pricing, generally available in July. CIO reported a price of $2 per successful resolution, with a 1,000-resolution minimum for prepurchased packs. On September 11, it listed Casey, its “help agent,” and Fin, its “customer agent,” as separate, generally available agents among seven new “job-ready” Agentforce agents. Salesforce’s service page calls Casey its Help Agent. Fin’s website fills in the other side. It lists compatibility with Salesforce, HubSpot, Freshworks, Dixa, Front, Zoho, Sprinklr, Gorgias and custom help desks, says setup takes under an hour without a migration, and prices the agent at $0.99 per outcome, with a 50-outcome monthly minimum, when it runs on a customer’s existing help desk. Those are vendor claims. Set beside Help Agent’s reported $2, they invite a comparison, but the two prices are not like for like, because each vendor defines a billable outcome differently. Salesforce says it does not charge when a customer asks for a human or walks away unhappy. Fin does not bill escalations either, but it does count a customer who exits without asking for more help as an assumed resolution. Salesforce’s September 11 release adds one more number. It says 79% of Anthropic’s conversations that Fin sees are resolved autonomously, one customer’s result among several the release lists rather than a platform average, and it says Fin is powered by Operator, a customer operations agent, and Fin Apex, a set of custom models. Agentforce is growing quickly without help. Salesforce reported $1.2 billion in Agentforce annual recurring revenue in its first fiscal quarter, up 205% year over year, and more than $1.5 billion in the second, up over 240%. Those figures argue against reading the deal as a patch for a weak product. One way to read it instead is as coverage: Salesforce now has an answer for the buyer who wants an agent running without a build project. McCabe framed the gain as distribution. “The big strategic benefit of our decision to join Salesforce is magnitudes more businesses and their customers that we can bring it to,” he said in the closing announcement. Marc Benioff, Salesforce’s chair and CEO, put it this way in the same release: “The #1 customer agent meets the #1 CRM.” Both rankings are Salesforce’s own claims. What Salesforce Still Has to Answer The first question is neutrality. Fin’s website lists compatibility with help desks from other vendors, including HubSpot, Freshworks and Zoho, and Salesforce says Fin “works seamlessly with the help desks and systems companies already use.” The promise is in the present tense, and the closing announcement names no rival platform. Opus Research, writing on September 25, reported that Fin works with rivals such as Zendesk and that Salesforce will keep selling the Intercom help desk. The second is packaging. Salesforce now sells Help Agent and Fin side by side, and neither the closing announcement nor the September 11 agent launch says how the two will be priced against each other. Customers choosing between them will want that settled before they commit. The third is competition. Sierra, which builds AI agents for customer-facing work including support, raised $950 million at a $15 billion valuation in May, according to SiliconANGLE. A venture round and a full acquisition are different transactions, so the two figures do not compare directly. They do point to how much capital is moving into this category. What to Watch Next Salesforce’s fiscal third-quarter results are the first period in which Fin is part of the company. If Salesforce breaks out Fin’s contribution, that number will say more than any launch announcement about whether buyers want a customer service agent bought rather than built. For customers already running Fin on a help desk that Salesforce does not own, the practical test is whether the compatibility Salesforce describes today is still there when their contracts come up for renewal.

items.title: Microsoft Retires Themes by Copilot in Outlook Starting in Mid-October 2026
items.summary: Microsoft is retiring Themes by Copilot in Outlook worldwide, with the removal starting in mid-October 2026 and expected to finish by late October 2026, according to the Microsoft 365 Message Center post MC1492954, published on October 9. The change applies to users with a Copilot license on new Outlook for Windows , Outlook for Android, Outlook for iOS, Outlook for Mac, and Outlook on the web. Once the retirement reaches an account, Themes by Copilot is removed from Outlook's settings. Copilot themes can no longer be selected, and anyone who switches to a different theme cannot go back to a Copilot one afterward. Microsoft gives no reason for the retirement in the message. Outlook users without a Copilot license are not affected by the change. What Happens to Existing Copilot Themes in Outlook A Copilot theme that is already applied stays in place until the user changes it. Themes set to refresh automatically also remain applied, but they stop refreshing and keep the imagery they show at the moment of the retirement. Themes by Copilot was offered to Copilot Pro and Microsoft 365 Copilot subscribers in the Appearance settings of Outlook. Users could start from a weather type or a location, either their own or one of more than 100 curated destinations, and then choose a realistic, oil painting, or cartoon art style. Each generated theme combined a wallpaper, shown as the background on desktop or at the top of the mobile apps, with a matching accent color for the rest of the interface. Refresh intervals ranged from every few hours to daily, weekly, or monthly. Microsoft launched a separate collection of standard themes, which are not AI-generated, for all Outlook users regardless of license status, with color options such as green, red, and purple. The retirement notice covers only Themes by Copilot. What Copilot License Holders Should Check in Outlook The Message Center post states that no action is required. Users who like their current Copilot wallpaper should still keep the following in mind before the removal arrives: Leave the current Copilot theme applied if the imagery should stay, since switching to any other theme removes the option to return. Expect auto-refreshing Copilot themes to freeze on their current image once the retirement reaches the account. Pick a replacement from the standard theme collection in Outlook's Appearance settings if a frozen image is not wanted. The removal comes shortly after Microsoft announced plans to block .msix attachments in new Outlook in November. Microsoft is rolling the retirement out gradually across the mid to late October window, so Themes by Copilot remains visible in Settings on some accounts until the removal reaches them. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

Microsoft is retiring Themes by Copilot in Outlook worldwide, with the removal starting in mid-October 2026 and expected to finish by late October 2026, according to the Microsoft 365 Message Center post MC1492954, published on October 9.

The change applies to users with a Copilot license on new Outlook for Windows, Outlook for Android, Outlook for iOS, Outlook for Mac, and Outlook on the web.

Once the retirement reaches an account, Themes by Copilot is removed from Outlook's settings. Copilot themes can no longer be selected, and anyone who switches to a different theme cannot go back to a Copilot one afterward.

Microsoft gives no reason for the retirement in the message. Outlook users without a Copilot license are not affected by the change.

What Happens to Existing Copilot Themes in Outlook

A Copilot theme that is already applied stays in place until the user changes it. Themes set to refresh automatically also remain applied, but they stop refreshing and keep the imagery they show at the moment of the retirement.

Themes by Copilot was offered to Copilot Pro and Microsoft 365 Copilot subscribers in the Appearance settings of Outlook. Users could start from a weather type or a location, either their own or one of more than 100 curated destinations, and then choose a realistic, oil painting, or cartoon art style.

Each generated theme combined a wallpaper, shown as the background on desktop or at the top of the mobile apps, with a matching accent color for the rest of the interface. Refresh intervals ranged from every few hours to daily, weekly, or monthly.

Microsoft launched a separate collection of standard themes, which are not AI-generated, for all Outlook users regardless of license status, with color options such as green, red, and purple. The retirement notice covers only Themes by Copilot.

What Copilot License Holders Should Check in Outlook

The Message Center post states that no action is required. Users who like their current Copilot wallpaper should still keep the following in mind before the removal arrives:

  1. Leave the current Copilot theme applied if the imagery should stay, since switching to any other theme removes the option to return.
  2. Expect auto-refreshing Copilot themes to freeze on their current image once the retirement reaches the account.
  3. Pick a replacement from the standard theme collection in Outlook's Appearance settings if a frozen image is not wanted.

The removal comes shortly after Microsoft announced plans to block .msix attachments in new Outlook in November.

Microsoft is rolling the retirement out gradually across the mid to late October window, so Themes by Copilot remains visible in Settings on some accounts until the removal reaches them.

items.title: Building a Production-Grade Dimensional Model on Snowflake with Cortex Code using Skills
items.summary: How I designed, audited, and expanded an e-commerce star schema using an AI-powered skill — and what I learned about letting the machine enforce Kimball principles. The Problem: Dimensional Modeling Is Tedious, Not Hard Every data engineer knows the drill. You need a star schema for analytics. You know the theory — grain first, conformed dimensions, surrogate keys, the whole Kimball playbook. But the execution? That’s 200 lines of DDL, manual constraint wiring, zero-value rows you’ll forget, and clustering keys you’ll second-guess. What if you could encode those decisions into a reusable skill that enforces best practices every time — and then let an AI agent execute it? That’s what I built. This article walks through the full journey: creating a Cortex Code skill for dimensional modeling, testing it against a real e-commerce schema, auditing it against best practices, and expanding it with three additional fact tables. What We’re Building 12 tables. 8 dimensions. 4 fact tables. 28 constraints. 20,000+ rows of sample data. Step 1: The Skill — Encoding Kimball Into a Reusable Agent Instead of writing one-off DDL, I created a Cortex Code skill called snowflake-dimensional-modeling. A skill is a markdown file (SKILL.md) with YAML frontmatter that tells the AI agent when to activate and how to behave. Here’s the core workflow: Two approval gates, two revision loops: model first, then DDL, then execute. The skill supports three modes: Design New — describe a business process, get a star schema Review & Improve — point it at existing tables, get an audit report Expand — add more fact tables to an existing model What the Skill Enforces Every invocation, regardless of mode, applies these principles: Grain first — the skill refuses to design dimensions until the grain is stated as a business sentence Conformed dimensions — reuses DIM_DATE and DIM_GEOGRAPHY across all facts Zero-value rows — every dimension gets SK=0 for late-arriving facts Informational constraints — PK/FK on everything so BI tools discover relationships Queryable documentation — COMMENT on every table and key column Audit columns — ETL_LOADED_AT and ETL_SOURCE on every table Step 2: The Build — From Natural Language to Running Schema I told the skill: “I want to model an e-commerce business. We have orders, products, customers, and payments. Key questions: revenue by product category and region, monthly order trends, customer lifetime value.” What It Designed Grain: One row per order line item Dimensions: DIM_DATE - generated, 2020-2027, calendar + fiscal DIM_CUSTOMER - SCD Type 2 (address changes matter for LTV) DIM_PRODUCT - SCD Type 1 (overwrite is fine) DIM_PAYMENT_METHOD - SCD Type 1 Fact: FACT_ORDER_LINE Clustered by (DATE_SK, PRODUCT_SK) Measures: quantity, unit_price, discount, line_total, tax Two design decisions worth noting: SCD Type 2 for customers, Type 1 for products. The skill chose Type 2 for customers because the user asked about LTV — you need address history to track customer migration across regions. Products don’t need history for this use case. Clustering on (DATE_SK, PRODUCT_SK). Date first because “monthly order trends” is a time-series query. Product second because “revenue by category” groups through the product dimension. Step 3: The Audit — What the Skill Caught After building the initial model, I ran the skill in Review mode. It ran four diagnostic queries and produced a severity-ranked report: Six audit findings: one orphan table, three warnings, two suggestions. The orphan table was a leftover from a previous task. The skill caught it because it checks for tables with no FK relationships and no audit columns — a table that doesn’t participate in any star schema relationship is suspicious. The Fix The skill applied all fixes in one pass: Dropped the orphan table Added PAYMENT_METHOD_ID natural key Extended retention to 7 days Added search optimization Created conformed DIM_GEOGRAPHY Added shipping measures to the fact Step 4: The Expansion — Three New Fact Tables The real test of a dimensional model is whether it grows gracefully. I asked the skill to expand with returns, inventory snapshots, and customer sessions. Fact Design Decisions Transaction facts record events. Snapshots record state. The row counts show it. FACT_RETURN links back to the original order via ORDER_NUMBER (degenerate dimension). This enables return rate analysis: "Which products have the highest return rate by category?" FACT_INVENTORY_SNAPSHOT is a periodic snapshot — the key insight is that its measures are semi-additive . You can SUM quantity_on_hand across products (how much total stock in a warehouse?) but you must AVG across time (what's the average stock level this month?). The skill marks this in the column COMMENT so BI tools don't accidentally SUM across dates. FACT_CUSTOMER_SESSION captures web behavior without requiring a purchase. This enables funnel analysis: sessions → products_viewed → added_to_cart → converted . The IS_CONVERTED flag and optional ORDER_NUMBER bridge to FACT_ORDER_LINE for attribution. Conformed Dimensions in Action The expansion added three new dimensions (DIM_WAREHOUSE, DIM_RETURN_REASON, DIM_TRAFFIC_SOURCE) but reused four existing ones. This is conformed dimensions working as designed — DIM_DATE appears in all four fact tables, DIM_PRODUCT in three, DIM_CUSTOMER in three. The payoff is cross-fact drill-across queries: -- Net revenue: orders minus refunds, by product SELECT p.PRODUCT_NAME, SUM(o.LINE_TOTAL) AS GROSS_REVENUE, SUM(r.REFUND_AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_REFUNDS, SUM(o.LINE_TOTAL) - SUM(r.REFUND_AMOUNT) AS NET_REVENUE FROM DIM_PRODUCT p LEFT JOIN FACT_ORDER_LINE o ON p.PRODUCT_SK = o.PRODUCT_SK LEFT JOIN FACT_RETURN r ON p.PRODUCT_SK = r.PRODUCT_SK WHERE p.PRODUCT_SK > 0 GROUP BY p.PRODUCT_NAME ORDER BY NET_REVENUE DESC; This query works because both facts share DIM_PRODUCT as a conformed dimension. Step 5: The Automation — Lint, Test, Publish I built three scripts to make the skill CI-friendly: lint-skill.sh — validates SKILL.md structure (frontmatter, sections, checkpoints, placeholder consistency, balanced code fences). Zero errors, zero warnings on the final version. test-skill.sh — integration tests against the live ECOMMERCE.ANALYTICS schema. Checks table existence (12 tables), row counts, constraint counts (28), zero-value rows in all dimensions, and a cross-fact join. publish-skill.sh — orchestrates lint → test → publish. Supports --dry-run, --roles, and --private flags. # Dry run: lint + test, don't publish ./scripts/publish-skill.sh --dry-run # Publish to account, discoverable by everyone ./scripts/publish-skill.sh --roles PUBLIC # Publish to specific roles only ./scripts/publish-skill.sh --roles ANALYST,DATA_ENG What I Learned 1. Skills Are Better Than Templates A SQL template gives you structure. A skill gives you judgment . The skill chose SCD Type 2 for customers because the user asked about LTV. It chose Type 1 for products because history wasn’t needed. A template can’t make that call. 2. The Audit Checklist Is the Real Value Designing a model from scratch is the easy part. Reviewing an existing one — finding the orphan tables, the missing natural keys, the DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1 — that's where the skill earns its keep. The nine-item audit checklist catches things humans skip. 3. Semi-Additive Measures Need Documentation Inventory snapshots are the most dangerous fact table type because they look additive but aren’t. Marking measures as semi-additive in the column COMMENT is a small thing that prevents significant downstream errors. 4. Conformed Dimensions Pay Off at Expansion Time When I added three fact tables, the model grew from 6 tables to 12. But I only added 3 new dimensions — the other 5 were reused. That’s the Kimball promise delivered: the shared dimensions enable cross-fact queries that would be impossible with isolated schemas. 5. UNIFORM() Has Constant-Bound Requirements Snowflake’s UNIFORM(min, max, RANDOM()) requires min and max to be constants, not column references. When generating sample data with dynamic bounds, you need to pre-compute random values in a CTE. A small gotcha that cost me one retry. The Final Model ECOMMERCE.ANALYTICS ├── 8 Dimensions (with zero-value rows, audit columns, informational constraints) │ ├── DIM_DATE — 2,922 rows (2020-2027, calendar + fiscal) │ ├── DIM_CUSTOMER — 21 rows (SCD Type 2, search optimized) │ ├── DIM_PRODUCT — 21 rows (SCD Type 1) │ ├── DIM_GEOGRAPHY — 21 rows (conformed, 6 regions) │ ├── DIM_PAYMENT_METHOD — 9 rows (with natural key) │ ├── DIM_WAREHOUSE — 6 rows (5 fulfillment centers) │ ├── DIM_RETURN_REASON — 9 rows (3 categories) │ └── DIM_TRAFFIC_SOURCE — 8 rows (6 mediums) ├── 4 Fact Tables (clustered, FK-constrained, grain-documented) │ ├── FACT_ORDER_LINE — 500 rows (transaction) │ ├── FACT_RETURN — 150 rows (transaction) │ ├── FACT_INVENTORY_SNAPSHOT — 18,400 rows (periodic snapshot) │ └── FACT_CUSTOMER_SESSION — 1,000 rows (transaction) └── 28 Constraints (8 PK + 20 FK) The skill is published to the Snowflake account and available to anyone with the share URI. Type /snowflake-dimensional-modeling in Cortex Code to start. Built with Cortex Code on Snowflake. The skill, scripts and DDL are available in the Github . items.summary_html:
How I designed, audited, and expanded an e-commerce star schema using an AI-powered skill — and what I learned about letting the machine enforce Kimball principles.The Problem: Dimensional Modeling Is Tedious, Not Hard

Every data engineer knows the drill. You need a star schema for analytics. You know the theory — grain first, conformed dimensions, surrogate keys, the whole Kimball playbook. But the execution? That’s 200 lines of DDL, manual constraint wiring, zero-value rows you’ll forget, and clustering keys you’ll second-guess.

What if you could encode those decisions into a reusable skill that enforces best practices every time — and then let an AI agent execute it?

That’s what I built. This article walks through the full journey: creating a Cortex Code skill for dimensional modeling, testing it against a real e-commerce schema, auditing it against best practices, and expanding it with three additional fact tables.

What We’re Building12 tables. 8 dimensions. 4 fact tables. 28 constraints. 20,000+ rows of sample data.Step 1: The Skill — Encoding Kimball Into a Reusable Agent

Instead of writing one-off DDL, I created a Cortex Code skill called snowflake-dimensional-modeling. A skill is a markdown file (SKILL.md) with YAML frontmatter that tells the AI agent when to activate and how to behave.

Here’s the core workflow:

Two approval gates, two revision loops: model first, then DDL, then execute.

The skill supports three modes:

  • Design New — describe a business process, get a star schema
  • Review & Improve — point it at existing tables, get an audit report
  • Expand — add more fact tables to an existing model
What the Skill Enforces

Every invocation, regardless of mode, applies these principles:

  1. Grain first — the skill refuses to design dimensions until the grain is stated as a business sentence
  2. Conformed dimensions — reuses DIM_DATE and DIM_GEOGRAPHY across all facts
  3. Zero-value rows — every dimension gets SK=0 for late-arriving facts
  4. Informational constraints — PK/FK on everything so BI tools discover relationships
  5. Queryable documentation — COMMENT on every table and key column
  6. Audit columns — ETL_LOADED_AT and ETL_SOURCE on every table
Step 2: The Build — From Natural Language to Running Schema

I told the skill: “I want to model an e-commerce business. We have orders, products, customers, and payments. Key questions: revenue by product category and region, monthly order trends, customer lifetime value.”

What It Designed
Grain: One row per order line item

Dimensions:
  DIM_DATE          - generated, 2020-2027, calendar + fiscal
  DIM_CUSTOMER      - SCD Type 2 (address changes matter for LTV)
  DIM_PRODUCT       - SCD Type 1 (overwrite is fine)
  DIM_PAYMENT_METHOD - SCD Type 1
  
Fact: FACT_ORDER_LINE
  Clustered by (DATE_SK, PRODUCT_SK)
  Measures: quantity, unit_price, discount, line_total, tax

Two design decisions worth noting:

SCD Type 2 for customers, Type 1 for products. The skill chose Type 2 for customers because the user asked about LTV — you need address history to track customer migration across regions. Products don’t need history for this use case.

Clustering on (DATE_SK, PRODUCT_SK). Date first because “monthly order trends” is a time-series query. Product second because “revenue by category” groups through the product dimension.

Step 3: The Audit — What the Skill Caught

After building the initial model, I ran the skill in Review mode. It ran four diagnostic queries and produced a severity-ranked report:

Six audit findings: one orphan table, three warnings, two suggestions.

The orphan table was a leftover from a previous task. The skill caught it because it checks for tables with no FK relationships and no audit columns — a table that doesn’t participate in any star schema relationship is suspicious.

The Fix

The skill applied all fixes in one pass:

  • Dropped the orphan table
  • Added PAYMENT_METHOD_ID natural key
  • Extended retention to 7 days
  • Added search optimization
  • Created conformed DIM_GEOGRAPHY
  • Added shipping measures to the fact
Step 4: The Expansion — Three New Fact Tables

The real test of a dimensional model is whether it grows gracefully. I asked the skill to expand with returns, inventory snapshots, and customer sessions.

Fact Design DecisionsTransaction facts record events. Snapshots record state. The row counts show it.

FACT_RETURN links back to the original order via ORDER_NUMBER (degenerate dimension). This enables return rate analysis: "Which products have the highest return rate by category?"

FACT_INVENTORY_SNAPSHOT is a periodic snapshot — the key insight is that its measures are semi-additive. You can SUM quantity_on_hand across products (how much total stock in a warehouse?) but you must AVG across time (what's the average stock level this month?). The skill marks this in the column COMMENT so BI tools don't accidentally SUM across dates.

FACT_CUSTOMER_SESSION captures web behavior without requiring a purchase. This enables funnel analysis: sessions → products_viewed → added_to_cart → converted. The IS_CONVERTED flag and optional ORDER_NUMBER bridge to FACT_ORDER_LINE for attribution.

Conformed Dimensions in Action

The expansion added three new dimensions (DIM_WAREHOUSE, DIM_RETURN_REASON, DIM_TRAFFIC_SOURCE) but reused four existing ones. This is conformed dimensions working as designed — DIM_DATE appears in all four fact tables, DIM_PRODUCT in three, DIM_CUSTOMER in three.

The payoff is cross-fact drill-across queries:

-- Net revenue: orders minus refunds, by product
SELECT
    p.PRODUCT_NAME,
    SUM(o.LINE_TOTAL) AS GROSS_REVENUE,
    SUM(r.REFUND_AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_REFUNDS,
    SUM(o.LINE_TOTAL) - SUM(r.REFUND_AMOUNT) AS NET_REVENUE
FROM DIM_PRODUCT p
LEFT JOIN FACT_ORDER_LINE o ON p.PRODUCT_SK = o.PRODUCT_SK
LEFT JOIN FACT_RETURN r ON p.PRODUCT_SK = r.PRODUCT_SK
WHERE p.PRODUCT_SK > 0
GROUP BY p.PRODUCT_NAME
ORDER BY NET_REVENUE DESC;

This query works because both facts share DIM_PRODUCT as a conformed dimension.

Step 5: The Automation — Lint, Test, Publish

I built three scripts to make the skill CI-friendly:

lint-skill.sh — validates SKILL.md structure (frontmatter, sections, checkpoints, placeholder consistency, balanced code fences). Zero errors, zero warnings on the final version.

test-skill.sh — integration tests against the live ECOMMERCE.ANALYTICS schema. Checks table existence (12 tables), row counts, constraint counts (28), zero-value rows in all dimensions, and a cross-fact join.

publish-skill.sh — orchestrates lint → test → publish. Supports --dry-run, --roles, and --private flags.

# Dry run: lint + test, don't publish
./scripts/publish-skill.sh --dry-run

# Publish to account, discoverable by everyone
./scripts/publish-skill.sh --roles PUBLIC

# Publish to specific roles only
./scripts/publish-skill.sh --roles ANALYST,DATA_ENG
What I Learned1. Skills Are Better Than Templates

A SQL template gives you structure. A skill gives you judgment. The skill chose SCD Type 2 for customers because the user asked about LTV. It chose Type 1 for products because history wasn’t needed. A template can’t make that call.

2. The Audit Checklist Is the Real Value

Designing a model from scratch is the easy part. Reviewing an existing one — finding the orphan tables, the missing natural keys, the DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1 — that's where the skill earns its keep. The nine-item audit checklist catches things humans skip.

3. Semi-Additive Measures Need Documentation

Inventory snapshots are the most dangerous fact table type because they look additive but aren’t. Marking measures as semi-additive in the column COMMENT is a small thing that prevents significant downstream errors.

4. Conformed Dimensions Pay Off at Expansion Time

When I added three fact tables, the model grew from 6 tables to 12. But I only added 3 new dimensions — the other 5 were reused. That’s the Kimball promise delivered: the shared dimensions enable cross-fact queries that would be impossible with isolated schemas.

5. UNIFORM() Has Constant-Bound Requirements

Snowflake’s UNIFORM(min, max, RANDOM()) requires min and max to be constants, not column references. When generating sample data with dynamic bounds, you need to pre-compute random values in a CTE. A small gotcha that cost me one retry.

The Final Model
ECOMMERCE.ANALYTICS
├── 8 Dimensions (with zero-value rows, audit columns, informational constraints)
│   ├── DIM_DATE           — 2,922 rows (2020-2027, calendar + fiscal)
│   ├── DIM_CUSTOMER       — 21 rows (SCD Type 2, search optimized)
│   ├── DIM_PRODUCT        — 21 rows (SCD Type 1)
│   ├── DIM_GEOGRAPHY      — 21 rows (conformed, 6 regions)
│   ├── DIM_PAYMENT_METHOD — 9 rows (with natural key)
│   ├── DIM_WAREHOUSE      — 6 rows (5 fulfillment centers)
│   ├── DIM_RETURN_REASON  — 9 rows (3 categories)
│   └── DIM_TRAFFIC_SOURCE — 8 rows (6 mediums)
├── 4 Fact Tables (clustered, FK-constrained, grain-documented)
│   ├── FACT_ORDER_LINE         — 500 rows (transaction)
│   ├── FACT_RETURN             — 150 rows (transaction)
│   ├── FACT_INVENTORY_SNAPSHOT — 18,400 rows (periodic snapshot)
│   └── FACT_CUSTOMER_SESSION   — 1,000 rows (transaction)
└── 28 Constraints (8 PK + 20 FK)

The skill is published to the Snowflake account and available to anyone with the share URI. Type /snowflake-dimensional-modeling in Cortex Code to start.

Built with Cortex Code on Snowflake. The skill, scripts and DDL are available in the Github.

items.title: How Did I Write My First FlashAttention Kernel in CUDA ?
items.summary: From demystifying the online softmax trick to hitting a 41.6x speedup on an NVIDIA RTX 4050 GPU — a beginner’s hands-on journey into hardware-aware deep learning. Transformers have completely reshaped the landscape of artificial intelligence. At the beating heart of every Transformer model lies the self-attention mechanism. It empowers language models to capture intricate contextual relationships across sequences. Yet, self-attention is simultaneously a double-edged sword: its algorithmic complexity is 𝒪(N²) , meaning memory consumption and computation explode quadratically as sequence lengths grow. Over the years, numerous researchers attempted to alleviate this burden using algorithmic approximation ( Sparse Attention , Linformer , Performer , etc.). While mathematically clever, many failed to dominate in practice because the quality trade-offs were unacceptable or they were not hardware-friendly. When purely algorithmic solutions hit a ceiling, researchers looked at the hardware. In 2022, Tri Dao et al. introduced FlashAttention — an exact attention algorithm that redesigns attention around GPU memory hierarchy and IO-awareness. │ Note: Throughout my learning and debugging journey, I paired with Google Antigravity as my AI pair programmer, which helped me unravel the math and pinpoint subtle GPU memory pitfalls. 1. The Core Bottleneck: GPU Memory Hierarchy To understand why FlashAttention is necessary, we must look at how modern GPUs operate. A GPU is not just a massive compute engine, it is a hierarchy of memory spaces with vastly different bandwidths: HBM / Global Memory (VRAM): Large (e.g., 6GB–80GB), but relatively slow (~1.5–3 TB/s on modern architectures). SRAM / Shared Memory & Registers: On-chip, blisteringly fast (~19 TB/s), but minuscule (around 48KB–228KB per Streaming Multiprocessor). 2. The Standard Attention Trap Standard attention computes: In standard frameworks (naive PyTorch or CUDA implementations): Compute X = QKᵀ / √d ∈ ℝᴺˣᴺ → Written to Global Memory (HBM). Read X back, compute A = softmax(X) ∈ ℝᴺˣᴺ → Written to Global Memory (HBM). Read A back, compute O = AV ∈ ℝᴺˣᵈ → Written to Global Memory (HBM). For a sequence length of N = 16, 384, an N × N matrix contains over 268 million floating-point number (over 1 GB of memory for just a single attention head). The GPU spends nearly all its time waiting to transfer bytes across the memory bus rather than computing floating-point operations. It is overwhelmingly memory bound. FlashAttention solves this via Kernel Fusion: it never materializes the N × N matrix in Global Memory. Everything stays on-chip in SRAM. 3. The Mathematical Magic: From Safe Softmax to FlashAttention Why couldn’t we simply tile attention like regular matrix multiplication?Because Softmax is not naturally associative. Traditional softmax ( link ) Safe softmax ( link ) To compute the denominator, you traditionally need to see all N elements first. This normally requires 3 passes over the data: Pass 1: Find the maximum m (to avoid numerical overflow in float16/float32). Pass 2: Calculate the sum of exponentials d = ∑ eˣʲ⁻ᵐ . Pass 3: Divide each element aᵢ = eˣⁱ⁻ᵐ / d . The Online Softmax Trick (from 3 passes to 2 passes) In 2018, Milakov & Gimelshein proved that you can maintain a running maximum and running denominator dynamically. If you have processed tokens up to index i — 1 with running max mᵢ₋₁ and denominator d′ᵢ₋₁, and you encounter a new element xᵢ by following those steps: Update running maximum: mᵢ = max(mᵢ₋₁, xᵢ) Update running denominator using the recurrence relation: dᵢ stands for sum of row i-th ( link ) FlashAttention’s AHA Moment Tri Dao noticed something brilliant: we do not actually need the attention matrix A! We only care about the final output vector O = AV. By defining a surrogate running output vector o′ᵢ: oᵢ stands for updated vector i-th ( link ) As we sweep through the sequence, we continuously rescale our running output vector and blend in the new token’s contribution. When we reach the final token o′ₙ , is mathematically identical to standard attention — computed entirely in a single pass without ever writing N × N scores to VRAM! 4. The Tiled FlashAttention Algorithm: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough Before writing a single line of CUDA code, let’s look at the high-level algorithm. The genius of FlashAttention lies in transforming a global operation over huge N × N matrices into iterative tile-by-tile computations. Here is the pseudo-algorithm from the paper: FlashAttention paper ( link ) How the Algorithm Works in 5 Core Steps Partitioning the inputs: Divide the large input matrices Q , K , and V from HBM into smaller blocks fitting directly into SRAM. Q and O are split into row blocks of size Bᵣ × d , while K and V are split into blocks of size B꜀ × d . Statistics vectors m (row maximums) and ℓ (row sum of exponentials) are initialized to -∞ and 0 . 2. Loading blocks into SRAM: Execute a double loop over the tiles. The outer loop loads a column block Kⱼ , Vⱼ into fast on-chip SRAM once. The inner loop iterates over row blocks, streaming Qᵢ , the current accumulator Oᵢ , and local statistics mᵢ , ℓᵢ into SRAM to process tile by tile without writing intermediate full attention matrices to VRAM. 3. Computing local attention logits: Multiply the current query block with the key block directly in SRAM: Sᵢⱼ = QᵢKⱼᵀ This produces a tiny Bᵣ × B꜀ tile of raw attention scores rather than the massive N × N matrix. 4. Applying the online softmax update: Find the local row maximum m̃ᵢⱼ = rowmax(Sᵢⱼ) and compute unnormalized exponentials P̃ᵢⱼ = exp(Sᵢⱼ — m̃ᵢⱼ) along with their row sums ℓ̃ᵢⱼ . Update the global row statistics on-chip using online softmax: mᵢⁿᵉʷ = max(mᵢ, m̃ᵢⱼ) ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ = eᵐⁱ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ ℓᵢ + eᵐ̃ⁱʲ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ ℓ̃ᵢⱼ 5. Trap 2: Loading K and V In my first draft, I attempted to load Key and Value rows into Shared Memory like this: s_k[tid][kv_idx] = K[global_kv_row * d + kv_idx]; // Bug! The Bug: Instead of copying the full head dimension vector ( d = 64 ), each thread copied only a single float at column kv_idx. This left the remaining 63 elements filled with uninitialized garbage data in Shared Memory, completely corrupting subsequent dot-product results. The Fix: I replaced the single assignment with an explicit loop across all d channels so each thread populates its complete row: for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) { s_k[tid][k] = K[global_kv_row * d + k]; s_v[tid][k] = V[global_kv_row * d + k]; } This guarantees the entire feature vector is loaded before computing attention scores. 6. __shared__ float s_k[KV_SIZE][D]; __shared__ float s_v[KV_SIZE][D]; int tid = threadIdx.x; // Each thread handles 1 row of Q int global_q_row = blockIdx.x * Q_SIZE + tid; int n_kv_blocks = (N + KV_SIZE - 1) / KV_SIZE; k < d; k++) { s_q[tid][k] = Q[global_q_row * d + k]; } __syncthreads(); // Step 2: Loop over all KV blocks for (int kv_idx = 0; kv_idx < n_kv_blocks; kv_idx++) { int global_kv_row = kv_idx * KV_SIZE + tid; // Load K and V tiles into Shared Memory (with bounds check) if (global_kv_row < N) { for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) { s_k[tid][k] = K[global_kv_row * d + k]; s_v[tid][k] = V[global_kv_row * d + k]; } } else { for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) { s_k[tid][k] = 0.0f; s_v[tid][k] = 0.0f; } } __syncthreads(); // Step 3: Compute Q * K^T for thread's row for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) { float sum = 0.0f; for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) { sum += s_q[tid][j] * s_k[i][j]; // Step 5: Safe exponentiation and tile sum float l_local = 0.0f; for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) { float p = expf(s_row[i] - m_new); s_row[i] = p; l_local += p; } // Step 6: Online Softmax updates float alpha = (m_global <= -1e20f) ? 0.0f : expf(m_global - m_new); float l_new = l_global * alpha + l_local; // Step 7: Rescale previous output vector float rescale_old = (l_global * alpha) / l_new; for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) { o[i] *= rescale_old; } // Step 8: Accumulate (P * V) / l_new float rescale_new = 1.0f / l_new; From demystifying the online softmax trick to hitting a 41.6x speedup on an NVIDIA RTX 4050 GPU — a beginner’s hands-on journey into hardware-aware deep learning.

Transformers have completely reshaped the landscape of artificial intelligence. At the beating heart of every Transformer model lies the self-attention mechanism. It empowers language models to capture intricate contextual relationships across sequences. Yet, self-attention is simultaneously a double-edged sword: its algorithmic complexity is 𝒪(N²), meaning memory consumption and computation explode quadratically as sequence lengths grow.

Over the years, numerous researchers attempted to alleviate this burden using algorithmic approximation (Sparse Attention, Linformer, Performer, etc.). While mathematically clever, many failed to dominate in practice because the quality trade-offs were unacceptable or they were not hardware-friendly.

When purely algorithmic solutions hit a ceiling, researchers looked at the hardware. In 2022, Tri Dao et al. introduced FlashAttention — an exact attention algorithm that redesigns attention around GPU memory hierarchy and IO-awareness.

│ Note: Throughout my learning and debugging journey, I paired with Google Antigravity as my AI pair programmer, which helped me unravel the math and pinpoint subtle GPU memory pitfalls.

1. The Core Bottleneck: GPU Memory Hierarchy

To understand why FlashAttention is necessary, we must look at how modern GPUs operate. A GPU is not just a massive compute engine, it is a hierarchy of memory spaces with vastly different bandwidths:

  • HBM / Global Memory (VRAM): Large (e.g., 6GB–80GB), but relatively slow (~1.5–3 TB/s on modern architectures).
  • SRAM / Shared Memory & Registers: On-chip, blisteringly fast (~19 TB/s), but minuscule (around 48KB–228KB per Streaming Multiprocessor).
2. The Standard Attention Trap

Standard attention computes:

In standard frameworks (naive PyTorch or CUDA implementations):

  1. Compute X = QKᵀ / √d ∈ ℝᴺˣᴺ → Written to Global Memory (HBM).
  2. Read X back, compute A = softmax(X) ∈ ℝᴺˣᴺ → Written to Global Memory (HBM).
  3. Read A back, compute O = AV ∈ ℝᴺˣᵈ → Written to Global Memory (HBM).

For a sequence length of N = 16, 384, an N × N matrix contains over 268 million floating-point number (over 1 GB of memory for just a single attention head). The GPU spends nearly all its time waiting to transfer bytes across the memory bus rather than computing floating-point operations. It is overwhelmingly memory bound.

FlashAttention solves this via Kernel Fusion: it never materializes the N × N matrix in Global Memory. Everything stays on-chip in SRAM.

3. The Mathematical Magic: From Safe Softmax to FlashAttention

Why couldn’t we simply tile attention like regular matrix multiplication?Because Softmax is not naturally associative.

Traditional softmax (link)Safe softmax (link)

To compute the denominator, you traditionally need to see all N elements first. This normally requires 3 passes over the data:

  • Pass 1: Find the maximum m (to avoid numerical overflow in float16/float32).
  • Pass 2: Calculate the sum of exponentials d = ∑ eˣʲ⁻ᵐ.
  • Pass 3: Divide each element aᵢ = eˣⁱ⁻ᵐ / d.
The Online Softmax Trick (from 3 passes to 2 passes)

In 2018, Milakov & Gimelshein proved that you can maintain a running maximum and running denominator dynamically. If you have processed tokens up to index i — 1 with running max mᵢ₋₁ and denominator d′ᵢ₋₁, and you encounter a new element xᵢ by following those steps:

  1. Update running maximum: mᵢ = max(mᵢ₋₁, xᵢ)
  2. Update running denominator using the recurrence relation:
dᵢ stands for sum of row i-th (link)FlashAttention’s AHA Moment

Tri Dao noticed something brilliant: we do not actually need the attention matrix A! We only care about the final output vector O = AV. By defining a surrogate running output vector o′ᵢ:

oᵢ stands for updated vector i-th (link)

As we sweep through the sequence, we continuously rescale our running output vector and blend in the new token’s contribution. When we reach the final token o′ₙ , is mathematically identical to standard attention — computed entirely in a single pass without ever writing N × N scores to VRAM!

4. The Tiled FlashAttention Algorithm: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough

Before writing a single line of CUDA code, let’s look at the high-level algorithm. The genius of FlashAttention lies in transforming a global operation over huge N × N matrices into iterative tile-by-tile computations.

Here is the pseudo-algorithm from the paper:

FlashAttention paper (link)How the Algorithm Works in 5 Core Steps
  1. Partitioning the inputs:

Divide the large input matrices Q, K, and V from HBM into smaller blocks fitting directly into SRAM. Q and O are split into row blocks of size Bᵣ × d, while K and V are split into blocks of size B꜀ × d. Statistics vectors m (row maximums) and ℓ (row sum of exponentials) are initialized to -∞ and 0.

2. Loading blocks into SRAM:

Execute a double loop over the tiles. The outer loop loads a column block Kⱼ, Vⱼ into fast on-chip SRAM once. The inner loop iterates over row blocks, streaming Qᵢ, the current accumulator Oᵢ, and local statistics mᵢ, ℓᵢ into SRAM to process tile by tile without writing intermediate full attention matrices to VRAM.

3. Computing local attention logits:

Multiply the current query block with the key block directly in SRAM:

Sᵢⱼ = QᵢKⱼᵀ

This produces a tiny Bᵣ × B꜀ tile of raw attention scores rather than the massive N × N matrix.

4. Applying the online softmax update:

Find the local row maximum m̃ᵢⱼ = rowmax(Sᵢⱼ) and compute unnormalized exponentials P̃ᵢⱼ = exp(Sᵢⱼ — m̃ᵢⱼ) along with their row sums ℓ̃ᵢⱼ. Update the global row statistics on-chip using online softmax:

mᵢⁿᵉʷ = max(mᵢ, m̃ᵢⱼ) ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ = eᵐⁱ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ ℓᵢ + eᵐ̃ⁱʲ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ ℓ̃ᵢⱼ

5. Updating the output accumulator (Oᵢ):

Rescale the previous partial output to align with the new max, add the contribution of the current tile P̃ᵢⱼVⱼ, and normalize by ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ:

Oᵢ ← diag(ℓᵢⁿᵉʷ)⁻¹ (diag(ℓᵢ)eᵐⁱ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ Oᵢ + eᵐ̃ⁱʲ⁻ᵐⁱⁿᵉʷ P̃ᵢⱼVⱼ)

Write updated Oᵢ, mᵢ, and ℓᵢ back to HBM for the next iteration.

5. The CUDA Architecture: Mapping the cordinates & memory flow

Translating the above theoretical algorithm to physical GPU hardware requires a rigorous understanding of the CUDA Memory Hierarchy and Thread Hierarchy:

Generated by GeminiWho does what on the GPU ?
  1. The CUDA grid: Work distribution
  • Tile-to-Block Mapping: Each CUDA block (blockIdx.x) processes exactly one row tile Qᵢ of size Bᵣ × d and computes its final output tile Oᵢ.
  • Grid Sizing: For a sequence length N = 1024 with block size Bᵣ = 64, we launch a 1D grid of 1024 / 64 = 16 blocks.

2. Threads within a block: Collaborative parallelism

  • Token Ownership: Each block contains Bᵣ = 64 threads (threadIdx.x = tid). Thread tid owns row tid of the Qᵢ tile, corresponding to one token in the sequence.
  • Coalesced Tile Loading: All 64 threads cooperate to stream Q, K, and V tiles from global memory (HBM) into Shared Memory (SRAM) using aligned memory transactions.
  • Race-Free Attention: Thread tid independently computes dot products between its query row and all key columns in Kⱼ, eliminating write conflicts and synchronization overhead.

3. Memory hierachy: Where data lives

  • Shared Memory (SRAM — Block Scope):
  • Holds tiles Qᵢ, Kⱼ, and Vⱼ (s_q, s_k, s_v).
  • Total footprint: 3 × 64 × 64 × 4 bytes = 48 KB (fits comfortably within the on-chip budget).
  • Registers (Private to Thread — Fastest):
  • m_global: Running maximum (1 float).
  • l_global: Running sum of exponentials (1 float).
  • o[D]: Output accumulator vector (64 floats for d = 64).
  • s_row[KV_SIZE]: Local attention logit tile.
6. The traps I fell into (And how I fixed them)

Writing CUDA kernels is humbling. Here are the real bugs I encountered and resolved:

Trap 1: Hardware shared memory limit

Initially, I allocated four tiles directly in Shared Memory: s_q, s_k, s_v, and s_s (each 64 × 64 × 4 bytes = 16 KB), totaling 64 KB.

When compiling, nvcc threw a hard fatal error:

ptxas error : Entry function uses too much shared data (0x10000 bytes, 0xc000 max)

The default hardware limit for statically allocated Shared Memory per thread block is 48 KB (0xc000), but my kernel requested 64 KB (0x10000).

The Fix: Notice that thread tid only ever reads its own row of attention logits during the online softmax update. There was zero cross-thread communication needed for matrix S:

  • Removed s_s from Shared Memory entirely.
  • Stored the intermediate attention scores in a thread-private local register array (float s_row[64]).

This eliminated 16 KB of SRAM, bringing total shared memory footprint to exactly 48 KB (3 × 16 KB) and fitting inside the default hardware budget.

Trap 2: Loading K and V

In my first draft, I attempted to load Key and Value rows into Shared Memory like this:

s_k[tid][kv_idx] = K[global_kv_row * d + kv_idx]; // Bug!

The Bug:

Instead of copying the full head dimension vector (d = 64), each thread copied only a single float at column kv_idx. This left the remaining 63 elements filled with uninitialized garbage data in Shared Memory, completely corrupting subsequent dot-product results.

The Fix:

I replaced the single assignment with an explicit loop across all d channels so each thread populates its complete row:

for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) {
    s_k[tid][k] = K[global_kv_row * d + k];
    s_v[tid][k] = V[global_kv_row * d + k];
}

This guarantees the entire feature vector is loaded before computing attention scores.

6. The working CUDA kernel

Here is the clean, working implementation of Tiled FlashAttention:

#define D 64        // Head dimension
#define Q_SIZE 64   // Block size for Q (Br)
#define KV_SIZE 64  // Block size for K, V (Bc)

__global__ void flash_attention(
    const float *Q, 
    const float *K, 
    const float *V,
    float *O, 
    int N, 
    int d
) {
    // 3 * 64 * 64 * 4 bytes = 48 KB (fits default Shared Memory limit)
    __shared__ float s_q[Q_SIZE][D];
    __shared__ float s_k[KV_SIZE][D];
    __shared__ float s_v[KV_SIZE][D];

    int tid = threadIdx.x; // Each thread handles 1 row of Q
    int global_q_row = blockIdx.x * Q_SIZE + tid;
    int n_kv_blocks = (N + KV_SIZE - 1) / KV_SIZE;
    float scale = 1.0f / sqrtf((float)d);

    // Online Softmax statistics in registers
    float m_global = -1e30f;
    float l_global = 0.0f;
    float o[D] = {0.0f};
    float s_row[KV_SIZE]; // Local attention logits for thread's row

    if (global_q_row < N) {
        // Step 1: Load Q tile into Shared Memory once
        for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) {
            s_q[tid][k] = Q[global_q_row * d + k];
        }
        __syncthreads();

        // Step 2: Loop over all KV blocks
        for (int kv_idx = 0; kv_idx < n_kv_blocks; kv_idx++) {
            int global_kv_row = kv_idx * KV_SIZE + tid;

            // Load K and V tiles into Shared Memory (with bounds check)
            if (global_kv_row < N) {
                for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) {
                    s_k[tid][k] = K[global_kv_row * d + k];
                    s_v[tid][k] = V[global_kv_row * d + k];
                }
            } else {
                for (int k = 0; k < d; k++) {
                    s_k[tid][k] = 0.0f;
                    s_v[tid][k] = 0.0f;
                }
            }
            __syncthreads();

            // Step 3: Compute Q * K^T for thread's row
            for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) {
                float sum = 0.0f;
                for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) {
                    sum += s_q[tid][j] * s_k[i][j];
                }
                s_row[i] = sum * scale;
            }

            // Step 4: Find local maximum in current tile
            float m_local = -1e30f;
            for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) {
                if (s_row[i] > m_local) {
                    m_local = s_row[i];
                }
            }
            float m_new = fmaxf(m_local, m_global);

            // Step 5: Safe exponentiation and tile sum
            float l_local = 0.0f;
            for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) {
                float p = expf(s_row[i] - m_new);
                s_row[i] = p;
                l_local += p;
            }

            // Step 6: Online Softmax updates
            float alpha = (m_global <= -1e20f) ? 0.0f : expf(m_global - m_new);
            float l_new = l_global * alpha + l_local;

            // Step 7: Rescale previous output vector
            float rescale_old = (l_global * alpha) / l_new;
            for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
                o[i] *= rescale_old;
            }

            // Step 8: Accumulate (P * V) / l_new
            float rescale_new = 1.0f / l_new;
            for (int i = 0; i < KV_SIZE; i++) {
                float p_val = s_row[i] * rescale_new;
                for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) {
                    o[j] += p_val * s_v[i][j];
                }
            }

            m_global = m_new;
            l_global = l_new;
            __syncthreads();
        }

        // Step 9: Write final output vector to Global Memory (HBM)
        for (int i = 0; i < d; i++) {
            O[global_q_row * d + i] = o[i];
        }
    }
}
7. Benchmarking & Evaluation

I evaluated the implementation on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4050 Laptop GPU with a sequence length of N = 1024 and head dimension d = 64:

 Implementation           | Execution Time (… | Speedup vs. CPU | Numerical Difference
--------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|-----------------------
 CPU Standard Attention   | 143.81 ms         | 1.0x (Baseline) | 0.0
 GPU Naive FlashAttention | 7.63 ms           | 18.8x           | 3.02 × 10⁻⁹
 GPU Tiled FlashAttention | 3.45 ms           | 41.6x           | 6.40 × 10⁻⁹
8. Lesson learned & Final thoughts

Writing this kernel taught me three core lessons:

  • Hardware awareness trumps raw FLOPs: Moving data costs significantly more latency and memory bandwidth than raw arithmetic. Minimizing round-trips to HBM is the defining factor behind high-performance deep learning systems.
  • Build from first principles: Progressing systematically from 3-pass Softmax to Online Softmax and finally to 1-pass FlashAttention breaks down a complex paper into clear, manageable steps.
  • Pair programming sharpens low-level engineering: Navigating hardware memory limits, thread synchronization, and floating-point stability can be daunting. Having an interactive thought partner to sanity-check equations and trace memory access patterns turns tedious debugging into a structured learning process.

If you are diving into CUDA or exploring how high-throughput inference engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and FlashAttention operate under the hood, there is no substitute for writing a kernel from scratch and profiling the execution yourself.

Happy coding!
